title: The Life of St. John of Shanghai and San Francisco
subtitle: In our own words, from the sources named under each part
source: A Life written by the Purify Team in its own words, each part with its sources named under it: the Orthodox Encyclopedia (vol. 23, 2012), the act of the commission on his relics (1993), the Orthodox Church in America's life of him, the Church Abroad's booklet of 2019 with the memoirs of Archbishop Peter of Chicago, Pascha in Summer (1996), the Holy Virgin Cathedral in San Francisco and the church of St. Job in Brussels, the United States Senate's hearings of 16 September 1949 and Public Law 81-555, L. Christoph's study of the refugees of Tubabao (2025), and OrthoChristian's report of 31 May 2024. The facts are theirs and the words are ours: nothing is copied or closely paraphrased from a Life under copyright. Where two sources differ, both are given.

sections.title: Michael Maximovitch
paragraphs: He was born Michael Maximovitch on 4 June 1896, at Adamovka in the Izium district of the province of Kharkov. His father, Boris Ivanovich, was the marshal of the nobility for his district; his mother was Glafira Mikhailovna, born Sevastianova. Michael was the eldest of their four children, with two brothers, Alexander and Constantine, and a sister, Maria. The family was the noble house from which St. John (Maximovich) of Tobolsk had come.

From 1907 to 1914 he studied in the cadet corps at Poltava. His parents chose the law for him over the theological academy at Kiev, and he read law at the University of Kharkov, graduating in 1918. In those years Archbishop Anthony (Khrapovitsky) became the guide of his life in the Church. During the Civil War he worked in the provincial court.
notes: Sources: the Orthodox Encyclopedia (Pravoslavnaya Entsiklopediya), vol. 23 (2012), pp. 230-238, under Ioann (Maksimovich); the Orthodox Church in America's life of him (Lives of the Saints, oca.org); the Holy Virgin Cathedral, San Francisco, on his life and the cathedral's history; Pascha in Summer (Paskha sredi leta), the Western European Diocese of the Church Abroad, 1996; the Church Abroad's booklet for the 25th year of his glorification (2019), with the memoirs of Archbishop Peter of Chicago.

sections.title: Exile, and the monastic life
paragraphs: In November 1920 he was evacuated from the Crimea to Constantinople, and in 1921 he came to the Kingdom of the Serbs, Croats and Slovenes. He studied theology at the University of Belgrade and graduated in 1925.

In 1924 Metropolitan Anthony made him a reader. In 1926, at the monastery of Milkovo, the Metropolitan tonsured him a monk and named him John, after St. John of Tobolsk, and the same year he was ordained deacon. On 21 November 1926 (4 December on the new calendar), the feast of the Entry of the Mother of God into the Temple, Bishop Gabriel (Chepur) ordained him priest.
From 1927 to 1934 he taught at the seminary at Bitola. There he began to serve the Divine Liturgy every day.
notes: Sources: the Orthodox Encyclopedia (Pravoslavnaya Entsiklopediya), vol. 23 (2012), pp. 230-238, under Ioann (Maksimovich); the Orthodox Church in America's life of him (Lives of the Saints, oca.org); Pascha in Summer (Paskha sredi leta), the Western European Diocese of the Church Abroad, 1996; the church of St. Job in Brussels, on St. John of Shanghai; the Church Abroad's booklet for the 25th year of his glorification (2019), with the memoirs of Archbishop Peter of Chicago.

sections.title: Bishop of Shanghai
paragraphs: On 3 June 1934 the Synod of Bishops of the Church Abroad chose him to be bishop of Shanghai, a vicar of the diocese of China and Peking, and on 10 June (28 May on the old calendar) he was consecrated in the Russian church of the Holy Trinity in Belgrade, Metropolitan Anthony presiding. He reached Shanghai on 4 December 1934, the feast of the Entry, eight years to the day from his ordination to the priesthood.

The cathedral of the icon of the Mother of God, Surety of Sinners, was finished under him. In his first year he founded an orphanage under the patronage of St. Tikhon of Zadonsk; over the years it took in more than two thousand children by one account, and about three thousand five hundred by another.

His own rule was severe, and the accounts agree on it. He served the services and received communion every day; he ate once a day, late in the day; he spent the nights in prayer and slept an hour or two, never lying down; he wore the poorest clothes, and often went barefoot. They differ on why he went barefoot. The Orthodox Church in America's life sees in it the way of a fool for Christ, who shuns honour. Archbishop Peter of Chicago, in his memoirs, rejects that name for it, and says he went barefoot indoors because sleeping upright had hurt his legs.

Under the Japanese occupation, after two leaders of the emigration had perished, he declared himself the acting head of the Russian colony. On 10 May 1946 the Council of Bishops of the Church Abroad raised him to archbishop.
notes: Sources: the Orthodox Encyclopedia (Pravoslavnaya Entsiklopediya), vol. 23 (2012), pp. 230-238, under Ioann (Maksimovich); the church of St. Job in Brussels, on St. John of Shanghai; the Orthodox Church in America's life of him (Lives of the Saints, oca.org); the Church Abroad's booklet for the 25th year of his glorification (2019), with the memoirs of Archbishop Peter of Chicago.

sections.title: Tubabao, and Washington
paragraphs: In 1949 the International Refugee Organization moved about five and a half thousand Russian refugees from Shanghai to a camp on the island of Tubabao, off Samar in the Philippines, where it stood until 1953; on 20 June 1949 it held 5,465 people. He left Shanghai with the last of them, on 4 May 1949. On Tubabao three temporary churches were set up for the camp.

He stayed in the Philippines until 11 July, reached San Francisco on 12 August, and went on to Jordanville. On 16 September 1949 he came before a subcommittee of the Senate's Committee on the Judiciary, in room 424 of the Senate Office Building, Senator Herbert O'Conor presiding. He was sworn as a witness, Dr Nicholas Alexander interpreted for him, and he spoke for the clause of the House bill H.R. 4567 that would let refugees from China into the United States, and for Senator Knowland's bill S. 666. The same month he founded the parish of St. John the Baptist in Washington.

The Senate passed the bill on 5 April 1950, and on 16 June 1950 it became law, with room for up to four thousand refugees from China. An American mission worked on Tubabao from August 1950 to February 1951; by 23 May 1951, 2,226 of the 2,465 people it had examined held visas for the United States. About 2,500 had left the island before then, most of them for Australia. The Synod of Bishops gave him a cross of diamonds to wear on his klobuk.
notes: Sources: L. Christoph, “Negotiating Refugee Futures”, Diasporas 44 (2025); the United States Senate, Committee on the Judiciary, hearings on displaced persons, 16 September 1949, pp. 379-391; the Orthodox Encyclopedia (Pravoslavnaya Entsiklopediya), vol. 23 (2012), pp. 230-238, under Ioann (Maksimovich); Public Law 81-555 of 16 June 1950 (64 Stat. 219); the Congressional Record, Daily Digest, 5 April 1950; the Eastern American Diocese of the Church Abroad, on the parish of St. John the Baptist in Washington; the Orthodox Church in America's life of him (Lives of the Saints, oca.org); the Church Abroad's booklet for the 25th year of his glorification (2019), with the memoirs of Archbishop Peter of Chicago.

sections.title: Archbishop in Western Europe
paragraphs: In 1950 he was appointed to Western Europe. He reached Paris on 21 July 1951 and lived first at Meudon, beside the church of the Resurrection, and from 1952 at Versailles, as Archbishop of Brussels and Western Europe. He served in French, in English and in Dutch, and in December 1961 he consecrated the church of All Saints of Russia in Paris.

In 1950 he wrote a report for the Synod on the veneration of the saints who shone in the West, and in his diocese the veneration of the Western saints who lived before the division of the Churches was restored.

On 11 November 1959 he received into the Church Abroad French communities that served in the Western rite, and on 11 November 1964 he and Bishop Theophil consecrated their leader, Jean-Nectaire (Kovalevsky), a bishop.
notes: Sources: the Orthodox Encyclopedia (Pravoslavnaya Entsiklopediya), vol. 23 (2012), pp. 230-238, under Ioann (Maksimovich); the church of St. Job in Brussels, on St. John of Shanghai; the Orthodox Church in America's life of him (Lives of the Saints, oca.org).

sections.title: San Francisco
paragraphs: On 4 December 1962 he came to San Francisco to govern the diocese for the ailing Archbishop Tikhon (Troitsky), who died on 30 March 1963. The new cathedral of the Mother of God, Joy of All Who Sorrow, whose ground had been broken on 25 June 1961, was still unfinished.

On 25 April 1963 the Synod recalled him to Western Europe, and many of the parishioners asked it to undo the decision. Those who opposed him went to the civil court in San Francisco, charging him with financial and administrative wrongdoing. The court ruled that church matters lay outside its competence, and the audit it ordered found nothing wrong on his part. On 14 August 1963 the Synod confirmed him in the see of San Francisco.
Under him the cathedral was finished, in November 1964; it was consecrated on 31 January 1977.
notes: Sources: the Orthodox Encyclopedia (Pravoslavnaya Entsiklopediya), vol. 23 (2012), pp. 230-238, under Ioann (Maksimovich); the Church Abroad's booklet for the 25th year of his glorification (2019), with the memoirs of Archbishop Peter of Chicago; the Holy Virgin Cathedral, San Francisco, on his life and the cathedral's history.

sections.title: His repose
paragraphs: On Saturday 2 July 1966 (19 June on the old calendar) he was in Seattle with the Kursk Root icon of the Mother of God, with which he was travelling. He served the Divine Liturgy that day at the cathedral of St. Nicholas, and reposed there. The room where he died is now a chapel.

The next day his body was flown to San Francisco, without being embalmed. Metropolitan Philaret, the First Hierarch of the Church Abroad, led his funeral in the cathedral, and he was laid in its crypt, beneath the altar. The Orthodox Encyclopedia gives 7 July for that; the Church Abroad's booklet of 2019 dates the burial to 11 July, after the city had changed its ordinance to allow it.
notes: Sources: the Orthodox Encyclopedia (Pravoslavnaya Entsiklopediya), vol. 23 (2012), pp. 230-238, under Ioann (Maksimovich); the Orthodox Church in America's life of him (Lives of the Saints, oca.org); the Church Abroad's booklet for the 25th year of his glorification (2019), with the memoirs of Archbishop Peter of Chicago; the church of St. Job in Brussels, on St. John of Shanghai.

sections.title: His glorification
paragraphs: In 1993 the Synod of Bishops of the Church Abroad decided to glorify him. A commission of its bishops began its work at his tomb on 30 September 1993 (17 September on the old calendar). Its act records that the coffin was opened at ten past ten at night on the feast of St. Chariton the Confessor, 11 October (28 September on the old calendar), and that his face and his hands were found incorrupt. On 1 July 1994 his relics were brought up into the cathedral, and on 2 July (19 June on the old calendar) the Council of Bishops of the Church Abroad glorified him there, Metropolitan Vitaly presiding.

On 24 June 2008 the Council of Bishops of the Russian Orthodox Church glorified him for veneration by the whole Church. On 30 May 2024, at the request of Metropolitan Nicholas, the First Hierarch of the Church Abroad, its Holy Synod added the feast of the uncovering of his relics to the calendar, on 12 October (29 September on the old calendar). He is remembered on 2 July, the day of his repose, and on 12 October.
notes: Sources: the act of the commission on his relics, 1993 (synod.com); the Orthodox Encyclopedia (Pravoslavnaya Entsiklopediya), vol. 23 (2012), pp. 230-238, under Ioann (Maksimovich); Pascha in Summer (Paskha sredi leta), the Western European Diocese of the Church Abroad, 1996; OrthoChristian, 31 May 2024.
